stem: A container writes uploaded files to `/app/uploads`, which is not a volume or mount. What happens to those files?

options.text: They are lost as soon as the container is stopped
options.why: Stopping keeps the writable layer; `docker start` brings the files back.

options.text: Kept through stop/start; deleted with `docker rm`
options.why: The writable layer belongs to the container and is deleted with it.

options.text: They are saved into the image, so new containers see them
options.why: Images are read-only; container changes never flow back without `docker commit`.

options.text: They are kept in an anonymous volume that outlives the container
options.why: No volume exists unless the image or the run command declares one.

explanation: Every container gets a thin writable layer on top of its image. It persists across `docker stop`/`docker start`, but `docker rm` deletes it. Data that must outlive the container belongs in a volume or bind mount.

stem: `docker stop` deletes the files a container has written to its writable layer.

options.text: True
options.why: Stopping only ends the processes; the writable layer stays on disk until the container is removed.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the layer is kept, so a restarted container still sees its files. Only `docker rm` deletes it.

explanation: A stopped container keeps its writable layer, its configuration and its logs. You can even `docker cp` files out of it. Data is lost only when the container is removed.

stem: Which kind of mount stores its data in a directory that Docker creates and manages (by default under `/var/lib/docker/volumes` on Linux)?

options.text: A named volume
options.why: Volumes live in Docker's storage area and are managed with `docker volume` commands.

options.text: A bind mount
options.why: A bind mount uses whatever host path you give it; Docker does not manage it.

options.text: A tmpfs mount
options.why: tmpfs lives in memory and never touches the host disk.

options.text: The container's writable layer
options.why: That lives inside the storage driver's directories and is deleted with the container.

explanation: Volumes are created and managed by Docker, which makes them portable, easy to back up and independent of the host's directory layout. Bind mounts depend on a specific host path, and tmpfs mounts are memory-only.

stem: Match each kind of container storage with its description.

options.text: Named volume
options.why: Docker-managed storage that outlives containers.

options.text: Bind mount
options.why: A host path mapped into the container.

options.text: tmpfs mount
options.why: Memory-only storage on Linux.

options.text: Writable layer
options.why: Per-container copy-on-write storage.

prompts.text: Managed by Docker, survives container removal, ideal for database files
Maps an exact host directory or file into the container, handy for live-editing source code
Held in memory only and gone when the container stops
Copy-on-write layer on top of the image, deleted with the container

explanation: Choose by lifetime and ownership: volumes for durable app data, bind mounts when the host must see or provide the files, tmpfs for temporary or sensitive data, and the writable layer only for disposable files.

stem: On a Linux host with the default data root, under which directory does the `local` volume driver keep volume data? Type the path.
explanation: Each volume lives at `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data`. `docker volume inspect` shows the exact path as `Mountpoint`. Don't edit it directly while containers are using it; go through a container instead.

stem: What does `docker run -v cache:/data alpine` mount at `/data`?

options.text: The host directory `./cache` from the current folder
options.why: A source without a slash is read as a volume name, not a path.

options.text: A tmpfs mount labelled `cache`
options.why: tmpfs needs `--tmpfs` or `--mount type=tmpfs`.

options.text: A named volume called `cache`, created if missing
options.why: With `-v`, a bare name is a volume name, and Docker creates the volume on first use.

options.text: An anonymous volume, with `cache` used only as a label
options.why: Anonymous volumes have no name; `cache` becomes the volume's actual name.

explanation: With `-v`, a first field starting with `/` (or a drive letter on Windows) is a host path for a bind mount; anything else is a volume name. Docker creates a missing named volume automatically.

stem: Which two commands mount the named volume `data` read-only at `/data`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `docker run -v data:/data:ro app`
options.why: The `ro` option makes the volume read-only inside the container.

options.text: `docker run --mount source=data,target=/data,readonly app`
options.why: `readonly` (or `ro`) is the `--mount` equivalent.

options.text: `docker run --read-only -v data:/data app`
options.why: `--read-only` makes the root filesystem read-only, not the volume.

options.text: `docker run -v data:/data:rw app`
options.why: `rw` is the default read-write mode.

options.text: `docker run --mount source=data,target=/data,mode=0444 app`
options.why: `--mount` has no `mode` option for volumes; file permissions are not a mount mode.

explanation: Read-only mounts are set per mount: `:ro` with `-v`, or `readonly`/`ro` in `--mount`. `--read-only` is a separate flag for the container's root filesystem, often paired with writable volumes or tmpfs mounts.

stem: Which job is a tmpfs mount best suited to?

options.text: Storing a database so that it survives a host reboot
options.why: tmpfs is in memory and is lost when the container stops.

options.text: Sharing build output between two running containers
options.why: tmpfs mounts can't be shared between containers.

options.text: Short-lived scratch files or secrets kept off disk
options.why: tmpfs keeps data in memory and drops it when the container stops.

options.text: Editing source code on the host with live reload
options.why: That needs a bind mount, so the host and container see the same files.

explanation: tmpfs mounts live in host memory, aren't written to the container's layer or the host filesystem, and vanish when the container stops. They suit caches, temporary files and sensitive data. They are Linux-only and can't be shared between containers.

stem:
The host directory `/srv/missing` does not exist. What happens with each command?

```bash
docker run -v /srv/missing:/data alpine true
docker run --mount type=bind,source=/srv/missing,target=/data alpine true
```

options.text: Both fail, because a bind mount needs an existing host path
options.why: Only `--mount` checks the path; `-v` creates the directory.

options.text: `-v` creates the directory; `--mount` fails: source missing
options.why: This is the documented difference between the two syntaxes for bind mounts.

options.text: Both create the directory, owned by the container's user
options.why: `--mount` refuses, and an auto-created directory is owned by root.

options.text: `--mount` creates the directory, but `-v` falls back to a volume
options.why: `-v` with an absolute path is always a bind mount.

explanation: For bind mounts, `-v` creates a missing host path as a directory owned by root. `--mount type=bind` instead fails because the source does not exist. The stricter behaviour catches typos that would otherwise mount an empty directory.

stem:
The `nginx` image contains `/usr/share/nginx/html/index.html`. What does the container serve in each case?

```bash
docker run -v site:/usr/share/nginx/html nginx          # site is a new, empty volume
docker run -v "$PWD/empty":/usr/share/nginx/html nginx  # empty host directory
```

options.text: The default page in both cases
options.why: A bind mount hides the image's files instead of copying them.

options.text: An empty site in both cases
options.why: An empty volume is first filled with the image's files.

options.text: Volume: the default page. Bind mount: an empty directory
options.why: Empty volumes are pre-populated from the image path; bind mounts hide it.

options.text: The bind mount shows the default page; the volume starts empty
options.why: It is the other way round: only volumes get the copy.

explanation: When an empty volume is mounted over a directory that has content in the image, Docker copies that content into the volume first. A bind mount never copies anything: it shows the host directory and hides whatever the image had at that path.

stem: An image declares `VOLUME /cache`. You run `docker run --rm -v reports:/reports image` and the container exits. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The anonymous volume created for `/cache` is removed
options.why: `--rm` deletes anonymous volumes along with the container.

options.text: The named volume `reports` still exists
options.why: Named volumes are never deleted by `--rm`.

options.text: Both volumes are removed, because `--rm` cleans up everything
options.why: `--rm` leaves named volumes alone so data isn't lost by accident.

options.text: Neither is removed, because `--rm` only deletes the writable layer
options.why: `--rm` also removes the container's anonymous volumes.

options.text: `reports` is removed if no other container ever used it
options.why: Docker never removes a named volume implicitly.

explanation: `docker run --rm` behaves like `docker rm -v`: the container and its anonymous volumes go, and named volumes stay. That is why databases should always use a named volume.

stem: On Docker Engine 23 or later, what does `docker volume prune` remove by default?

options.text: Every volume that no running container is using
options.why: Stopped containers still count as users, and named volumes are kept without `--all`.

options.text: Only anonymous volumes that no container uses
options.why: Since Engine 23 named volumes need `--all` (`-a`).

options.text: All unused named and anonymous volumes
options.why: That needs `docker volume prune --all`.

options.text: Volumes older than 24 hours, whatever their type
options.why: Pruning has no default age filter; `--filter` adds one.

explanation: Engine 23 (API 1.42) made `docker volume prune` safer: by default it removes only unused anonymous volumes. Add `--all` to include unused named volumes too. A volume referenced by any container, even a stopped one, is never pruned.

stem: Put the steps for backing up the data in container `db` (mounted at `/var/lib/data`) to `backup.tar` on the host in order.

options.text: Stop writes to the data, for example by stopping `db`
Start a throwaway container with `--volumes-from db` and a bind mount of the current host directory at `/backup`
Inside it, run `tar cvf /backup/backup.tar /var/lib/data`
Check `backup.tar` on the host, then restart `db`

explanation: The documented pattern is `docker run --rm --volumes-from db -v $(pwd):/backup ubuntu tar cvf /backup/backup.tar /var/lib/data`. `--volumes-from` gives the helper the same volumes, and the bind mount carries the archive out to the host. Stopping writes first gives a consistent copy.
reference: Docker docs: Back up, restore, or migrate data volumes

stem: An image runs as UID 1000. You start it with `-v /srv/app-data:/data`, where `/srv/app-data` did not exist beforehand. Writes to `/data` fail with "Permission denied". What is the cause?

options.text: Bind mounts are read-only unless you add `:rw`
options.why: Bind mounts are read-write by default.

options.text: Docker created the directory as root, so UID 1000 can't write
options.why: `-v` auto-creates missing paths as root-owned directories.

options.text: Containers can't write to host paths outside `/var/lib/docker`
options.why: Bind mounts can expose any host path.

options.text: The image's `USER` instruction blocks every mounted path
options.why: `USER` only sets the process UID; normal permissions decide the rest.

explanation: Permissions on a bind mount are the host directory's own permissions, checked against the container process's UID and GID. The auto-created directory belongs to root, so UID 1000 can't write. Fix it by `chown 1000:1000` on the host directory, or by running with a matching `--user`.

stem: Without user-namespace remapping, files that a container running as root writes into a bind mount appear on the host owned by root.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: UIDs pass through unchanged, so UID 0 in the container is UID 0 on the host.

options.text: False
options.why: They are root-owned on the host, which is why such files are hard to delete without sudo.

explanation: By default, containers share the host's UID space. Files created through a bind mount keep the numeric UID of the process that wrote them. Run as a non-root `--user`, or enable userns-remap or rootless mode, to avoid root-owned files in your project folders.

stem: What does `docker system df` report?

options.text: Docker's disk use: images, containers, volumes, cache
options.why: It summarises Docker's own disk usage by type, with reclaimable space.

options.text: Free space on every filesystem currently mounted on the host machine
options.why: That is the plain `df` command.

options.text: Disk reads and writes per container in real time
options.why: That is the block I/O column of `docker stats`.

options.text: Only the space taken by the image layers
options.why: Containers, volumes and build cache are listed too.

explanation: `docker system df` shows space per object type and how much is reclaimable. `docker system df -v` breaks it down per image, container and volume, which is the quickest way to find a runaway volume or build cache.

stem: With `--mount type=volume,...`, which option stops Docker from copying the image's existing files into a new, empty volume? Type the option name.
explanation: `volume-nocopy` (or `:nocopy` with `-v`) turns off pre-population, so the container sees the empty volume. Use it when the image's files at that path are not meant to seed the data.

stem: On Docker Desktop for Mac, `npm install` inside a container is very slow when the project is bind-mounted from the Mac. Which change usually helps the most?

options.text: Mount the project read-only so Docker skips change tracking
options.why: npm must write `node_modules`, so read-only fails, and sharing still has costs.

options.text: Move the project into `/tmp` on the Mac before mounting it
options.why: Any Mac path still goes through the same file-sharing layer to the Linux VM.

options.text: Keep `node_modules` in a named volume inside the VM
options.why: The heavy writes then avoid crossing the Mac-to-VM file-sharing boundary.

options.text: Run with a larger `--shm-size` to speed up file writes
options.why: Shared memory size does not affect file I/O on a bind mount.

explanation: Docker Desktop runs containers in a Linux VM. Bind mounts from macOS or Windows go through a file-sharing layer that is much slower for many small files. Named volumes live inside the VM's filesystem, so putting write-heavy directories in a volume avoids that cost.
reference: Docker docs: Docker Desktop file sharing

stem: Which two statements about tmpfs mounts are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Their data is gone when the container stops
options.why: tmpfs is never written to disk, so nothing survives a stop.

options.text: They can't be shared between containers
options.why: Each tmpfs mount belongs to one container.

options.text: They persist across `docker restart` like the writable layer
options.why: A restart stops the container, which drops the tmpfs contents.

options.text: Another container can reach them with `--volumes-from`
options.why: `--volumes-from` copies volume mounts, not tmpfs mounts.

options.text: They work the same on Windows containers
options.why: tmpfs mounts are only available for Linux containers.

explanation: tmpfs mounts are temporary, in memory, Linux-only and private to one container. Use them for scratch space or secrets, never for data that must survive a stop.

stem:
A team runs their dev container like this. Why is the second `-v` there?

```bash
docker run -v "$PWD":/app -v /app/node_modules my-node-app
```

options.text: It makes `node_modules` read-only to protect it from edits
options.why: No `ro` option is given, so the volume is writable.

options.text: An anonymous volume masks it, keeping the image's modules
options.why: Without it, the bind mount would hide the dependencies installed at build time.

options.text: It shares the host's `node_modules` with the container
options.why: That is the opposite: the point is to stop the host folder showing through.

options.text: It saves the dependencies back into the image
options.why: Volumes never change images.

explanation: The bind mount of `$PWD` hides the image's `/app`, including `node_modules` installed at build time. A volume mounted at the more specific path `/app/node_modules` takes precedence there. Because it starts empty, Docker pre-populates it from the image, so the container keeps its Linux-built dependencies while the source code stays live-editable.

stem: The `mysql` image declares `VOLUME /var/lib/mysql`. You run `docker run -d --name db mysql`, load data, then run `docker rm -f db` and start a new container with the same command. The database is empty. Where did the data go?

options.text: It was deleted with the container's writable layer
options.why: The data dir is a volume, not part of the writable layer.

options.text: In an orphaned anonymous volume; the new container got a new one
options.why: `docker rm` without `-v` keeps the old anonymous volume, but nothing reuses it.

options.text: MySQL wiped the directory on start because the container name was reused
options.why: MySQL doesn't react to container names.

options.text: It was moved into the image cache and needs `docker commit` to restore
options.why: Volume data is never merged into images.

explanation: Each `docker run` of an image with a `VOLUME` instruction creates a new anonymous volume unless you mount something there. `docker rm -f` without `-v` leaves the old volume dangling with your data, but the new container gets a fresh one. Use a named volume (`-v mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql`) so every container reattaches to the same data.

stem: Following on from a database container whose data now sits in an orphaned anonymous volume, which three actions are sound? (Choose three.)

options.text: List candidates with `docker volume ls -f dangling=true`
options.why: Dangling volumes are ones no container references.

options.text: Mount the right one into a new container to check and recover the data
options.why: An anonymous volume can be mounted by its ID like any volume.

options.text: Use a named volume from now on, so new containers reattach to the same data
options.why: That prevents the problem from happening again.

options.text: Run `docker volume prune` first to tidy up before searching
options.why: That would delete the dangling volume holding the data.

options.text: Recreate the container with the same name, which reattaches its old volume
options.why: Container names have no link to anonymous volumes.

explanation: Anonymous volumes are only identified by a hash, so find dangling ones, inspect or mount them to find the data, then copy or reuse it. Avoid prune commands until the data is safe, and switch to a named volume.

stem: A container bind-mounts a single file: `-v "$PWD/app.conf":/etc/app/app.conf`. You edit `app.conf` in an editor that saves by writing a temp file and renaming it over the original. The container keeps reading the old settings. Why?

options.text: Bind mounts are copied once at container start
options.why: Bind mounts are live, not copies.

options.text: A file mount pins the old inode; renaming swaps in a new one
options.why: Mount the directory instead, or edit the file in place.

options.text: The container caches every file it has read until it is restarted
options.why: There is no such cache; reads hit the mounted file.

options.text: Single-file bind mounts are read-only snapshots taken at start
options.why: They are read-write and live by default.

explanation: A bind mount attaches to an inode. Editors that save atomically write a new file and rename it, which swaps in a new inode on the host. The container still has the old one mounted. Mounting the parent directory avoids this, because directory lookups always find the current file.

stem:
A team keeps several apps' data in one named volume, `shared`, and wants each container to see only its own folder. They run:

```bash
docker run -d --mount type=volume,src=shared,dst=/data,volume-subpath=billing myapp
```

The `billing` folder has never been created inside the volume. What happens?

options.text: Docker creates the missing `billing` folder in the volume and mounts it
options.why: Unlike a missing bind-mount host path with `-v`, a missing volume subpath is not created for you.

options.text: The mount fails, because the subdirectory must exist in the volume first
options.why: The volume-subpath option mounts an existing subdirectory and errors when it is missing.

options.text: The container starts with the whole `shared` volume mounted at `/data` instead
options.why: Docker does not silently fall back to mounting the volume root when the subpath is missing.

options.text: The container starts with an empty anonymous volume at `/data` instead
options.why: No replacement volume is created; the requested mount simply cannot be set up.

explanation: `volume-subpath` (a `--mount` option for volumes) mounts one subdirectory of a volume, which is useful for sharing a single volume while giving each container a slice of it. The Docker docs state that the subdirectory must exist in the volume before the volume is mounted; if it doesn't, the mount fails and the container doesn't start. Create it first, for example by running a one-off container that mounts the whole volume and runs `mkdir /data/billing`.
reference: Docker docs: Volumes (Mount a volume subdirectory)

stem: An image ships a 2 GB data file. A container changes a single byte of it. What does the `overlay2` storage driver do?

options.text: Writes just the changed block into the container layer
options.why: overlay2 works at file level, not block level.

options.text: Edits the file in place in the image layer
options.why: Image layers are read-only.

options.text: Copies the whole file up into the writable layer first
options.why: This "copy-up" makes the first write slow and doubles the space used.

options.text: Refuses the write, because image files are read-only to containers
options.why: Writes succeed through copy-on-write.

explanation: overlay2 is file-level copy-on-write. The first write to a file from a lower layer copies the entire file up into the container's layer. For large or write-heavy files that is slow and wasteful, so such data belongs in a volume, which bypasses the storage driver.

stem: Two database server containers are started with the same named volume mounted as their data directory, to "share the load". What is the main risk?

options.text: Docker locks the volume, so the second container fails to start
options.why: Docker doesn't lock volumes; several containers can mount one.

options.text: The second container sees the volume read-only
options.why: Both mounts are read-write unless you ask otherwise.

options.text: Uncoordinated writes from two servers can corrupt the data
options.why: Database engines expect exclusive ownership of their data directory.

options.text: None: the volume driver merges both servers' writes safely
options.why: The local driver does no coordination at all.

explanation: Sharing a volume only shares files. A database server assumes it alone owns its data files, caches and write-ahead log. Two servers writing the same directory can corrupt it. Scale databases with replication, not shared data directories.

stem: Which command creates a volume backed by the NFS export `/exports/data` on server `10.0.0.5`, using the built-in `local` driver?

options.text: `docker volume create --driver nfs --opt server=10.0.0.5 --opt path=/exports/data --opt options=rw,hard nfsdata`
options.why: There is no built-in `nfs` driver; `local` handles NFS through mount options.

options.text: `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/data nfsdata`
options.why: This matches the documented `type`, `o` and `device` options.

options.text: `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt device=10.0.0.5:/exports/data nfsdata`
options.why: Without `o=addr=…` the NFS client is missing the server address option.

options.text: `docker volume create -v 10.0.0.5:/exports/data:/data nfsdata`
options.why: `docker volume create` has no `-v` flag.

explanation: The `local` driver passes options to `mount`: `type` is the filesystem, `o` the mount options (including the server address) and `device` the remote path, written with a leading colon. The NFS share is mounted when a container first uses the volume.

stem: Match each command with what it removes on Docker Engine 23 or later.

options.text: Unused anonymous volumes only
Unused anonymous and named volumes
Stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache, but no volumes
The same as above plus unused anonymous volumes

explanation: Volumes hold data, so prune commands are conservative with them. `docker system prune` never touches volumes unless you add `--volumes`, and even then only anonymous ones by default. Named volumes need `docker volume prune --all` or an explicit `docker volume rm`.
reference: Docker docs: Prune unused Docker objects

stem: `docker cp` can copy files out of a container that has already stopped.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: it reads the container's filesystem, which still exists after it stops.

options.text: False
options.why: It works on stopped containers, which is handy for grabbing logs or crash dumps after a failure.

explanation: `docker cp` works with running and stopped containers alike, because the writable layer and the mounted volumes persist until the container is removed.

stem: A service writes a decrypted API key to a file at start-up. Why is putting that file on a tmpfs mount better than the writable layer?

options.text: tmpfs encrypts its contents with a per-container key
options.why: tmpfs is plain memory; it has no encryption.

options.text: The key never reaches the host disk and disappears when the container stops
options.why: The writable layer lives on disk and survives until the container is removed.

options.text: Processes in other containers can't read tmpfs, but can read the writable layer
options.why: Other containers can't read either one directly.

options.text: `docker commit` copies tmpfs contents into images safely
options.why: tmpfs is excluded from commits, which is the point, not a safe copy.

explanation: The writable layer is stored on the host's disk, shows up in `docker diff` and `docker commit`, and lives until the container is removed. A tmpfs mount keeps the file in memory only and drops it on stop. The docs note tmpfs pages can still be swapped, so it reduces exposure rather than eliminating it.

stem: `docker run -v newvol:/app/data image` is run, where `newvol` doesn't exist yet and the image has files in `/app/data`. Put the events in order.

options.text: Docker creates the empty named volume `newvol`
Docker sees the volume is empty and the image path has content
The image's files at `/app/data` are copied into the volume
The volume is mounted at `/app/data` and the main process starts

explanation: Pre-population happens once, when an empty volume is first mounted over a non-empty directory. After that the volume's own contents win, even if a later image version ships different files at the same path.

stem: On an SELinux-enforcing host, a container gets "Permission denied" on a bind mount even though UIDs and modes are correct. Which two mount options relabel the content so the container can use it? (Choose two.)

options.text: `:z`, which applies a shared label usable by several containers
options.why: Shared relabelling suits content mounted into many containers.

options.text: `:Z`, which applies a private label for this container only
options.why: Private relabelling locks the content to one container.

options.text: `:ro`, which makes the mount read-only
options.why: Read-only doesn't change SELinux labels.

options.text: `:rshared`, which sets bind propagation
options.why: Propagation controls submounts, not security labels.

options.text: `:delegated`, which relaxes consistency
options.why: That is a legacy Docker Desktop hint and is ignored on Linux.

explanation: SELinux checks labels as well as UNIX permissions. `:z` relabels the host content with a shared container label, `:Z` with a private one. Be careful: relabelling system directories such as `/home` or `/usr` can break the host.

stem: Container `api` has stopped but still exists, and it mounts the volume `uploads`. What happens with `docker volume rm uploads`?

options.text: The volume is removed, because no container is running
options.why: A stopped container still counts as using the volume.

options.text: Docker removes the volume and recreates it empty next time
options.why: Docker won't remove it at all while the container exists.

options.text: It fails because the volume is in use; remove `api` first
options.why: Docker refuses to delete volumes referenced by any container, running or not.

options.text: Docker detaches the volume from `api` and then deletes it
options.why: Docker never edits a container's mounts after creation.

explanation: Volumes are protected while any container references them, including stopped ones. Remove the container first (`docker rm api`), then the volume, or use `docker rm -v` for anonymous volumes.

stem: A dev setup mounts `-v nm:/app/node_modules` (a named volume) next to the source bind mount. After adding a dependency to `package.json` and rebuilding the image, the container fails with "Cannot find module". Why?

options.text: The rebuild didn't install anything, because `npm ci` ignores new packages
options.why: The image does contain the package after the rebuild.

options.text: The non-empty `nm` volume isn't re-filled from the new image
options.why: Pre-population happens only into an empty volume, so the old modules shadow the new ones.

options.text: Named volumes are read-only after their first mount
options.why: Volumes stay writable.

options.text: The bind mount of the source overrides every nested mount
options.why: The more specific `node_modules` mount still wins at its own path.

explanation: Docker copies image content into a volume only when the volume is empty. Once `nm` holds dependencies from the old image, new images can't update it, and its stale contents hide the newly installed package. Remove the volume (or use an anonymous one recreated per container), or run the install at container start.

stem: On Windows with the WSL 2 backend, a project lives on `C:\code\app` and is bind-mounted into a container running a file-watching dev server. Edits from a Windows editor don't trigger reloads. What fix do Docker's docs recommend?

options.text: Add `:consistent` to the bind mount so events are delivered
options.why: That legacy option has no effect on file events.

options.text: Raise `fs.inotify.max_user_watches` in the container
options.why: The watch limit isn't the problem; the events never arrive.

options.text: Keep the project in the WSL 2 Linux filesystem
options.why: Files on the Linux side get native inotify events and much faster I/O.

options.text: Mount the folder as a named volume instead of a bind mount
options.why: A volume can't be edited directly by the Windows editor.

explanation: Bind mounts from the Windows filesystem cross into the Linux VM through a translation layer that is slow and unreliable for file-change notifications. Docker recommends storing projects in the WSL 2 distribution's filesystem, or falling back to the watcher's polling mode.
reference: Docker docs: Docker Desktop WSL 2 best practices

stem: A nightly job backs up a busy PostgreSQL container by running `tar` over its data volume while the database keeps running. Restores sometimes fail to start or lose recent rows. What is the core problem?

options.text: `tar` can't read files that a running container has open
options.why: tar reads them fine; that is the danger.

options.text: The volume should have been backed up with `docker commit`
options.why: Commit ignores volume contents entirely.

options.text: A live file copy is inconsistent; use DB backup tools instead
options.why: Files change mid-copy, so the archive mixes different points in time.

options.text: The backup must run inside the same container to share its page cache
options.why: Where tar runs doesn't make the copy consistent.

explanation: A database writes many files and a log continuously. A file-by-file copy made while it runs can capture pages from different moments, which a restore may reject or replay incorrectly. Use the engine's own tools (`pg_dump`, `pg_basebackup`), stop the container first, or take an atomic filesystem snapshot.
reference: Docker docs: Back up, restore, or migrate data volumes

stem: A Dockerfile runs `RUN mkdir /data && chown app:app /data` and then `USER app`. Starting with `-v /srv/data:/data` gives "Permission denied", but `-v appdata:/data` with a new named volume works. Why the difference?

options.text: `USER` is ignored whenever a bind mount is present at start-up
options.why: `USER` always applies; ownership is what differs.

options.text: The bind mount shows host ownership; the volume kept `app`'s
options.why: Pre-population keeps the image's ownership; a bind mount hides it.

options.text: Named volumes ignore file permissions
options.why: Volumes enforce permissions like any filesystem.

options.text: The `chown` only applies to build steps, not to running containers
options.why: The ownership is part of the image layer and is present at run time.

explanation: A bind mount replaces `/data` with the host directory, so the image's `chown` is invisible and the host's ownership applies. An empty named volume is filled from the image path, keeping its ownership and permissions, so `app` can write. With bind mounts, fix ownership on the host or match `--user`.

stem: A container runs with `--tmpfs /scratch` and a job writes large temporary files there. What risk does this setup carry by default?

options.text: Writes fail once `/scratch` reaches 64 MB
options.why: That 64 MB default belongs to `/dev/shm`, not to tmpfs mounts.

options.text: No default size limit, so it can exhaust memory
options.why: Set `tmpfs-size` (or `size=` with `--tmpfs`) to cap it.

options.text: Files spill onto the host disk under `/var/lib/docker` when memory is low
options.why: tmpfs never spills into Docker's storage area.

options.text: The mount is shared with every container on the host
options.why: Each tmpfs mount is private to its container.

explanation: Docker's tmpfs mounts default to an unlimited size and mode 1777. Data written there is held in memory, so a runaway writer can exhaust it and trigger the OOM killer. Always set a size for tmpfs used by untrusted or heavy workloads.

stem: Which three practices are sound for running a production database in a container? (Choose three.)

options.text: Keep the data directory on a named volume or dedicated storage
options.why: Data then outlives containers and avoids copy-on-write overhead.

options.text: Allow a long enough stop timeout so the engine can shut down cleanly
options.why: The default is 10 seconds before SIGKILL, which can be too short.

options.text: Back up with the engine's own tools and test restores
options.why: Logical or base backups are consistent; copied files may not be.

options.text: Keep data in the writable layer so the container is self-contained
options.why: It is lost with the container and slowed by copy-on-write.

options.text: Use `docker commit` regularly as the backup method
options.why: Commit skips volumes and doesn't give consistent database backups.

options.text: Bind-mount the data from Docker Desktop on a laptop for speed
options.why: Desktop bind mounts are the slowest option, and laptops aren't production storage.

explanation: Treat the database container as replaceable and the data as precious: put it on durable storage, stop it gracefully (`--stop-timeout`), and back it up with tools that understand the engine.

stem: You need to move a service's data from the bind mount `/srv/legacy` to a new named volume `appdata` with minimal risk. Put the steps in order.

options.text: Stop the service so the data stops changing
Create the volume with `docker volume create appdata`
Run a helper container mounting `/srv/legacy` and `appdata`, and copy the files across, keeping ownership
Start the service with `-v appdata:/data` and verify the data
Only after checking, archive or delete `/srv/legacy`

explanation: Stop writes first so the copy is consistent, copy with a helper container (for example `cp -a`, which keeps ownership and modes), switch the service over, and keep the old data until you have verified the new setup.
reference: Docker docs: Back up, restore, or migrate data volumes

stem: In octal, what file mode does Docker give a tmpfs mount when you don't set `tmpfs-mode`? Type the number.
explanation: The default mode is 1777: world-writable with the sticky bit, like `/tmp`. Set `tmpfs-mode` (for example `700`) when only one user should access the mount.

stem: A CI runner's disk keeps filling up even though a nightly job runs `docker system prune -af`. Each pipeline runs `docker run` (without `--rm`) on an image that declares `VOLUME /cache`. What explains it?

options.text: `-a` makes prune skip images that are less than a day old
options.why: `-a` removes all unused images regardless of age.

options.text: Each run leaves an anonymous volume that system prune skips
options.why: The volumes pile up even after their containers are pruned.

options.text: Build cache can only be removed with `docker image prune`
options.why: `docker system prune` does include the build cache.

options.text: Stopped containers are kept for 24 hours before prune removes them
options.why: Prune removes all stopped containers immediately.

explanation: Every container from an image with a `VOLUME` instruction gets its own anonymous volume. Pruning the container doesn't delete it, and `docker system prune` leaves volumes alone unless you pass `--volumes`. Use `--rm` in CI, or prune volumes as well.
reference: Docker docs: Prune unused Docker objects

stem: An image contains a 5 GB log file baked into a lower layer. A running container deletes it with `rm`. How does host disk usage change?

options.text: It drops by 5 GB, because overlay2 frees the file's blocks
options.why: The file still belongs to a read-only image layer.

options.text: No: a whiteout hides it but the image layer keeps it
options.why: Deleting a lower-layer file only hides it from the container.

options.text: It grows by 5 GB, because the file is copied up before deletion
options.why: Deleting creates a small whiteout entry, not a copy.

options.text: It drops after `docker commit` turns the change into a layer
options.why: A committed layer adds a whiteout; it still doesn't shrink lower layers.

explanation: Image layers are immutable. Deleting a file that came from a lower layer adds a whiteout marker in the container's layer, which hides the file but leaves the bytes in place. Only rebuilding the image without the file reclaims the space.

stem: Why do write-heavy workloads such as databases perform better on a volume than in the container's writable layer? (Choose two.)

options.text: Volumes bypass the storage driver and its copy-on-write overhead
options.why: Writes go straight to the host filesystem.

options.text: Changing an existing file in a lower layer forces a full copy-up first
options.why: The writable layer pays that cost the first time each file is changed.

options.text: Volumes cache every write in memory and flush later
options.why: Volumes use the normal page cache; there is no extra write-back layer.

options.text: The writable layer is synced to the image on every write
options.why: Nothing is written back to the image.

options.text: Volumes are compressed, so less data reaches the disk
options.why: Local volumes aren't compressed.

explanation: Storage drivers like overlay2 add copy-on-write work and are optimised for image layering, not heavy random writes. Volumes are plain host directories (or driver-backed storage), giving native filesystem performance.

stem: An app expects its config at `/etc/app/config.yml`. You run `docker run -v "$PWD/config.yml":/etc/app/config.yml app`, but `config.yml` doesn't exist in the current directory. What happens?

options.text: Docker creates an empty `config.yml` file on the host and mounts it
options.why: Docker can't know you meant a file, so it creates a directory.

options.text: The run fails immediately because the source file is missing
options.why: That is `--mount`'s behaviour; `-v` creates the missing path.

options.text: Docker creates a directory named `config.yml`, and the app fails
options.why: With `-v`, missing paths are always created as directories.

options.text: The image's own `/etc/app/config.yml` is used as a fallback
options.why: The mount is still applied, hiding the image's file.

explanation: Because `-v` auto-creates missing host paths as directories, a typo or missing file turns into a directory named like the file, and the app then fails with an "is a directory" error. `--mount type=bind` would have failed fast with a clear missing-source error.
